document.title: Afghanistan: Jalaluddin Haqqani's Emergence As a Key Taliban Commander (Islama 00154)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
document.note: [Confidential] Haqqani is reported to be more liberal on social policy than other Taliban but lacks political clout, and is respected as a military commander. His ties to radical Arab groups concern State, as he reportedly offers shelter to Arabs in Paktia in exchange for weapons and money. Excised.

persons.name: Jalaluddin Haqqani
persons.role: Taliban 'Acting Minister of Tribes and Borders'; reportedly in charge of Taliban forces north of Kabul; former Hezb-i-Islami (Khalis) commander
persons.status_detail: Aged 50 in January 1997 per the cable

mentions.quote: FORMER AFGHAN RESISTANCE COMMANDER JALALUDDIN HAQQANI MAY NOW BE IN CHARGE OF THE TALIBAN'S FORCES NORTH OF KABUL
HIS FORMAL TALIBAN TITLE REMAINS "ACTING MINISTER OF TRIBES AND BORDERS."
HAQQANI, 50, HAS BEEN A COMMANDER FOR THE TALIBAN SINCE THE GROUP'S BEGINNING IN 1994.
HAQQANI IS "OFFERING SHELTER FOR VARIOUS ARABS IN AREAS OF PAKTIA PROVINCE."

persons.name: Mullah Borjan

persons.status_detail: Killed near Kabul in late September 1996

events.description: Taliban formed; Haqqani a commander since the group's beginning

Founding of the Taliban; Haqqani became a commander from the group's beginning.

sources_cited: Conversations with Abdul Wahab, a Taliban supporter, and General Payenda
key_claims: Haqqani may now be in charge of Taliban forces north of Kabul, succeeding the late Mullah Borjan, though the Taliban have not confirmed it.
Haqqani's formal Taliban title is Acting Minister of Tribes and Borders.
Haqqani is seen as influential in military strategy but not in Taliban political or social policy.
Haqqani reportedly has close ties to radical Arab groups from the jihad and shelters Arabs in Paktia in exchange for weapons and money.
Some Taliban officials such as Mullah Ghaus oppose Haqqani's extremist ties and downplay his importance.
Anti-Taliban Supreme Defense Council sees Haqqani's rise as a Taliban policy of placing hard men in key military positions, and expects tensions with undisciplined Zadran forces.
